pageData.title: The Safavid Empire
pageData.para1: The Safavid Empire. The Safavid Empire (1501-1736) is where modern Iran begins - the dynasty that made Iran a Shia Muslim nation and one of the great 'gunpowder empires' of the early modern world. In 1501 the young Shah Ismail I, carried to power by his fanatical Qizilbash - the 'red-head' Turkoman tribesmen - proclaimed Twelver Shi'ism the official religion of his empire. It was one of the great turning points in the history of Islam: Iran, until then largely Sunni, became the heartland of the Shia, and the sectarian geography of the Middle East was fixed into our own time.
pageData.para2: The early shahs warred constantly with the Sunni Ottomans and Uzbeks on their borders. Under Shah Tahmasp the empire began a profound transformation: to break the Qizilbash's grip on the army, the shahs imported hundreds of thousands of Georgians, Circassians, and Armenians from the Caucasus as ghulams - royal slaves trained for war and government, much like the Ottoman janissaries - who rose to the highest offices of the state.
pageData.para3: The dynasty's zenith came under Shah Abbas the Great (r. 1588-1629). He completed the ghulam army, built an artillery corps with European help, moved his capital to Isfahan, and revived the Silk Road through Iran, opening direct trade with England and the Netherlands in silk, carpets, and textiles. Isfahan under Abbas became one of the showpieces of the world, and Safavid Persia an economic stronghold between East and West, its court a rich mix of Turkoman lords, Persian bureaucrats, and Caucasian soldiers and courtiers.
pageData.para4: The end came with shocking speed: in 1722 Afghan tribesmen besieged and took Isfahan itself, and the once-mighty empire collapsed. The conqueror Nader Shah drove out the Afghans and briefly restored the Safavids as puppets before taking the throne himself in 1736. But the Safavid imprint on Iran was permanent: the Shia faith, the efficient state, and the architectural glories of Isfahan remain the dynasty's living legacy.

pageData.title: The Afsharid & Zand Dynasties
pageData.para1: The Afsharid and Zand Dynasties. Between the fall of the Safavids and the rise of the Qajars, 18th-century Iran passed through two short, vivid dynasties: the Afsharid empire of the conqueror Nader Shah (1736-1796) and the gentler Zand dynasty (1751-1794) of Karim Khan. Together they form the violent, brilliant interlude of modern Iranian history.
pageData.para2: Nader Shah was one of the most astonishing soldiers of the age: born into a poor semi-nomadic family of the Afshar tribe in Khorasan, he rose from local warlord to expel the Afghan invaders, recover Iran's lost provinces from the Ottomans and Russians, and in 1736 crown himself Shah. Under him Iran reached its greatest extent since the ancient Sasanians - from the Caucasus to Central Asia. His most famous campaign was the invasion of Mughal India: at Karnal in 1739 he crushed a Mughal army six times the size of his own, took Delhi, and carried off the imperial treasury - some seven hundred million rupees, the Peacock Throne, and the Koh-i-Noor and Daria-i-Noor diamonds.
pageData.para3: But Nader's later years darkened into cruelty, and in 1747 he was assassinated by his own officers. His empire shattered at once: Ahmad Shah Abdali founded the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan, and an Afsharid rump clung on only in Khorasan until 1796. Into the vacuum stepped Karim Khan Zand, who from 1751 ruled most of Iran - not as Shah but under the modest title Vakil ol-Ra'aya, 'regent of the people.' His twenty-eight-year reign was a rare interval of stability between the era of Nader's conquests and the rise of the Qajars.
pageData.para4: Karim Khan's death in 1779 unleashed civil war among his heirs. The last Zand, the young and chivalrous Lotf Ali Khan, fought a doomed resistance against the rising Qajar chieftain Agha Mohammad Khan and was defeated and deposed in 1794. With him ended the age of Nader and Karim Khan - and began the century of the Qajars.

pageData.title: The Qajar Empire
pageData.para1: The Qajar Empire. The Qajar dynasty (1789-1925) ruled Iran through the age of European empire - a reign of glittering courts and shrinking borders, in which Iran lost the Caucasus to Russia, escaped colonization by a hair's breadth, and ended by giving itself a constitution. It was founded by the formidable Agha Mohammad Khan, chieftain of the Qajar tribe, who defeated every rival of the Zand and Afsharid age, made his capital at Tehran, and was crowned Shah in 1796 - only to be assassinated the following year.
pageData.para2: His nephew Fath-Ali Shah inherited a fatal contest: Russia was advancing into the Caucasus, which Iran had ruled for centuries. Two disastrous wars settled it. By the Treaty of Gulistan (1813) Iran ceded Georgia, Dagestan, and most of Azerbaijan; by the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828), after Russia took Tabriz, it gave up the entire South Caucasus, and the border was fixed on the Aras River - where it remains. Iran's attempt to recover Herat in Afghanistan ended with the Treaty of Paris (1857), dictated by Britain.
pageData.para3: The long 19th century was the era of the Great Game: Russia pressing from the north, Britain from the Gulf and India, both extracting concessions while Qajar Iran maintained a precarious independence. Pressure produced change: in 1906 the Constitutional Revolution forced the Shah to grant the National Consultative Assembly - the Majlis - and Iran became a constitutional monarchy. The great powers answered in 1907 by formally dividing the country into Russian and British spheres of influence.
pageData.para4: The dynasty, weakened by war and the turmoil that followed, did not survive the aftermath of the First World War. In 1925 the Constituent Assembly deposed the last Qajar shah, Ahmad Shah, and transferred the crown to Reza Khan, founder of the Pahlavi dynasty. The Qajar age closed - but it left modern Iran its capital, its borders, and its constitution.

pageData.title: Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia
pageData.para1: Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia. For four centuries, from 1516 to 1918, the Arab lands of Syria and Mesopotamia were provinces of the Ottoman Empire - an era that shaped their cities, their sectarian geography, and ultimately their modern borders. The era began with Sultan Selim I's lightning campaign of 1516-1517: victory over the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq near Aleppo gave him Syria; the following year Egypt itself fell, and the Arab heartlands passed from Cairo to Constantinople.
pageData.para2: Ottoman Syria - the whole country between the Taurus mountains and Sinai - was governed from Damascus, then divided into the eyalets of Aleppo, Tripoli, and Sidon; Mount Lebanon won special autonomous status as early as 1667. The 19th century brought both reform and tragedy: the Tanzimat decrees of 1839 and 1856 declared Muslims and non-Muslims equal, but the old hierarchy's collapse fed sectarian violence - massacres of Christians at Aleppo in 1850 and, worst of all, in Damascus and Mount Lebanon in 1860. European pressure then forced the creation of the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate in 1861, an autonomous Christian-governed province - the seed of modern Lebanon. By the 1870s the region was organized into the vilayets of Syria, Aleppo, and Beirut, with Jerusalem an autonomous mutasarrifate.
pageData.para3: Mesopotamia followed its own rhythm. Suleiman the Magnificent conquered Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534, and for three centuries Iraq was the contested frontier of the Ottoman-Persian wars - Baghdad even fell to the Safavids from 1623 to 1638 before the Ottomans recovered it. From 1749 to 1831 the region was governed by a semi-autonomous dynasty of Georgian Mamluks ruling in the sultan's name; after their removal, the reforming governor Midhat Pasha modernized the provinces of Mosul, Baghdad, and Basra.
pageData.para4: The First World War ended Ottoman rule in both lands: British forces took Baghdad in 1917 and swept through Palestine and Syria in 1918. The empire's Arab provinces became British and French mandates - Iraq, Palestine, Syria, and Lebanon - and the borders drawn in those years are the borders on the map today.

pageData.title: The Ottoman Empire
pageData.para1: The Ottoman Empire. The Ottoman Empire (c. 1299-1922) was one of the longest-lived empires in world history: for over six centuries the House of Osman ruled from Constantinople at the crossroads of Europe and the Middle East, at its height holding lands on three continents. It began around 1299 as a tiny beylik on the Byzantine frontier in northwestern Anatolia, founded by the Turkoman leader Osman I. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326; by mid-century the Ottomans were in the Balkans, breaking Serbian power at Kosovo in 1389 - and even catastrophe, Timur's crushing victory at Ankara in 1402, only delayed them for a generation.
pageData.para2: The empire's two defining conquests came a century apart. In 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the thousand-year Byzantine Empire and making the city his capital; in 1517 Selim I destroyed the Mamluks, and the Ottoman sultans assumed the title of caliph, leaders of the Islamic world. Under Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566) - conqueror of Belgrade, victor of Mohacs, master of Baghdad - the empire became a global power, its laws and its armies the envy and terror of Europe. Its millions of Christian and Jewish subjects lived under the millet system, managing their own communal affairs.
pageData.para3: Modern historians date the long decline from the failed second siege of Vienna in 1683. The empire fell behind Europe technologically, lost wars and provinces to Austria and Russia, and watched new Balkan nations break away. Yet the 19th century also brought serious reform - the Tanzimat era, constitutional experiments, and finally the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 - before the Balkan Wars and the First World War brought the end: defeat, the Arab Revolt, genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks, and Allied partition.
pageData.para4: The sultanate was abolished in November 1922; the Republic of Turkey rose from its ruins under Mustafa Kemal Ataturk in 1923, and the caliphate itself was abolished in 1924. The Ottoman imprint endures everywhere its borders ran: in the nations of the Balkans and the Arab world, in Istanbul's skyline, and in the modern Republic of Turkey itself.

pageData.title: The Tulip Period & Early Reforms
pageData.para1: The Tulip Period and Early Reforms. The Tulip Period (1718-1730) was the Ottoman Empire's first opening to the West - a dozen years of peace, flowers, and fountains that began the empire's long, reluctant transformation. It opened with the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718, which ended a generation of war with Austria, and it took its name from the tulip craze that swept the court of Sultan Ahmed III: tulips filled the palaces, the gardens, the fabrics, and the poetry of Istanbul's elite.
pageData.para2: The man of the age was the Grand Vizier, Nevsehirli Damat Ibrahim Pasha, the sultan's son-in-law. Under his guidance the empire oriented itself outwards: trade and industry were promoted, and Ottoman public buildings took on Western European elements for the first time - the beginning of Ottoman Baroque architecture. Most momentous of all, the 1720s saw the establishment of the first Ottoman-language printing press, more than two centuries after printing had transformed Europe.
pageData.para3: But the elegance rested on a fragile base. The luxury of the court enraged the capital's soldiers and preachers, and in September 1730 the Patrona Halil revolt swept Ibrahim Pasha and the Tulip Age away. Yet the question the period had posed - how could the empire catch up with Europe? - would not go away. Sultan Selim III (r. 1789-1807) made the first major attempt to modernize the army; the Janissary corps, jealous of its privileges, revolted and destroyed him.
pageData.para4: The answer came in blood: Selim's successor, the dynamic Mahmud II, eliminated the Janissary corps in 1826, removing the greatest obstacle to reform and clearing the road to the Tanzimat. The Tulip Period's brief flowering had shown that Ottoman renewal was possible; the destruction of the Janissaries showed what it would cost.

pageData.title: The Tanzimat Era
pageData.para1: The Tanzimat Era. The Tanzimat - the 'Reorganization' (1839-1876) - was the Ottoman Empire's great attempt to save itself by reinventing itself: four decades in which reforming sultans and statesmen tried to build a modern, centralized, law-governed state on European lines, while holding a multinational empire together. It began on November 3, 1839, when the young Sultan Abdulmejid I issued the Edict of Gulhane, promising all his subjects - Muslim, Christian, and Jew alike - security of life, honor, and property, fair taxation and conscription, and public trials, and abolishing the notorious system of tax farming.
pageData.para2: The driving force was a generation of reformist statesmen - Mustafa Resid Pasha, Ali Pasha, and Fuad Pasha - who had served as ambassadors in London and Paris and believed European institutions could restore Ottoman power. Under them the empire gained ministries, secular Nizamiye courts alongside the religious ones, a modern school system capped by the Darulfunun, its first telegraph lines and railways, and codified laws for the millets, the empire's religious communities. The Imperial Reform Edict of 1856 went further still, proclaiming full legal equality for non-Muslims - the principle of Ottomanism, one citizenship for all the sultan's subjects.
pageData.para3: Reform had its price. The changes met resistance from conservative clerics, sharpened ethnic tensions in the Balkans, and were paid for with foreign loans - the first borrowed in 1858 to finance the Crimean War - that saddled the empire with crippling debt. Yet the momentum carried to its logical end: in 1876, amid the Great Eastern Crisis, Midhat Pasha and his allies deposed Sultan Abdulaziz and proclaimed the Ottoman constitution, opening the First Constitutional Era.
pageData.para4: The Tanzimat's legacy is still contested: some historians credit it with creating a powerful modern state and a new Ottoman identity; others argue it accelerated the empire's fragmentation. What is certain is that it transformed the empire's government, law, and daily life - and that every later Ottoman and Turkish reform, down to the Republic itself, built on its foundations.

pageData.title: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus
pageData.para1: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus. The Russian conquest of the Caucasus was one of the longest and bloodiest colonial wars of the 19th century - a half-century struggle (1817-1864) that brought the mountain peoples of the North Caucasus under the Tsar at a terrible human cost. Russia's advance began with the kingdoms south of the mountains: in 1801 it annexed the Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, and two victorious wars with Qajar Persia - sealed by the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828) - gave it the whole South Caucasus, from Dagestan to Armenia.
pageData.para2: The mountains themselves were another matter. The Caucasian War pitted the Russian Imperial Army and Cossack settlers against the Adyghe (Circassians), Chechens, Dagestanis, Abazins, and Ubykhs. In the east, the mountaineers found a leader of genius in Imam Shamil, who from 1834 held the empire at bay for a quarter-century - in 1843 capturing nearly every Russian outpost in Avaria in a single month, in 1845 withstanding Prince Vorontsov's great offensive. It took an army of 250,000 under General Baryatinsky to break the resistance; Shamil was captured in 1859 and exiled to central Russia.
pageData.para3: In the west, the war against the Circassians continued to 1864 - and ended in catastrophe for its victims. The conquest was accompanied by what is now called the Circassian genocide: the massacre, expulsion, and exile of the Circassian people to the Ottoman Empire. Kabardia's population fell from some 350,000 before the war to 50,000; at the Ottoman port of Samsun alone, up to 110,000 refugees huddled in camps where hundreds died daily. Cossack and Russian colonists were settled on the confiscated lands, remaking the region's ethnic map. On 21 May 1864, Tsar Alexander II declared the war over.
pageData.para4: The conquest left deep scars - a Circassian diaspora scattered across the Middle East, and grievances that erupted again in the 20th century. It also entered world literature: Pushkin's 'Prisoner of the Caucasus,' Lermontov's poems, and Tolstoy's tales of war were all born in those mountains.

pageData.title: The Kazakh Khanate
pageData.para1: The Kazakh Khanate. The Kazakh Khanate (1465-1847) was the last great nomadic state of the Eurasian steppe - the empire of the Kazakh people, heirs of the Golden Horde, who ruled the vast grasslands of what is now Kazakhstan for nearly four centuries. It was founded around 1465 by Kerei and Janibek, two princes who broke away from the fragmenting Uzbek Khanate to carve out their own realm on the steppe - the first nation-state in Central Asia created by a modern ethnic group itself.
pageData.para2: The khanate was a true nomadic empire: its power was the horse, the felt yurt, and the great tribal confederations. Over the 17th century the Kazakhs organized themselves into three hordes or zhuz - the Senior, the Middle, and the Junior - each with its own territory and seasonal migrations. After the death of Tauke Khan in the early 18th century, the zhuz became effectively independent khanates, and the unity of the steppe was lost.
pageData.para3: The brief restoration came under Ablai Khan, who reunified the Kazakhs and skillfully balanced the two empires closing in on the steppe - Russia from the north and Qing China from the east. After his death in 1781 the khanate fractured again, and this time the Russian advance could not be stopped: in 1822-1824 the Tsar's government abolished the khanate institution itself by statute, placing the steppe under direct imperial administration.
pageData.para4: The Kazakhs answered with their last national rising: Kenesary Qasymuly proclaimed himself khan in 1837 and fought Russian rule for ten years until his death in 1847. With him ended four centuries of steppe empire - the last chapter of the world the Mongols had made. The steppe passed under the Tsars, and the Kazakhs began the long road that would lead, a century and a half later, to an independent Kazakhstan.

pageData.title: The Uzbek Khanate
pageData.para1: The Uzbek Khanate. The Uzbek Khanate was the power that remade Central Asia at the close of the Timurid age - and its successor states, the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva, and Kokand, ruled the oases of Turkestan until the Russian Empire swallowed them in the 19th century. The Uzbeks were steppe nomads of the Golden Horde's successor world, welded into a khanate in the 15th century by the Chinggisid prince Abu'l-Khayr. His grandson Muhammad Shaybani led them to empire: in 1500-1501 he conquered Transoxiana - Samarkand, Bukhara, Tashkent, and Balkh - from the last Timurids, founding the Khanate of Bukhara.
pageData.para2: Under the Shaybanids and their successors the Janids (from 1599), Bukhara - made the permanent capital by Abdullah Khan II in 1562 - gave its name to the state, ruling Transoxiana's ancient cities of Samarkand, Tashkent, and Balkh. In 1740 the conqueror Nader Shah overran the khanate; after his death the Manghit clan seized power, and in 1785 Shah Murad replaced the khanate with the Emirate of Bukhara - its rulers taking the title emir since, not being descended from Genghis Khan, they could not claim the title of khan.
pageData.para3: To the west, in the ancient land of Khwarazm, the Khanate of Khiva (1511-1920) ruled from the walls of Khiva, surviving as an Afsharid vassal in the 1740s and later as a Russian protectorate from 1873. To the east, the Khanate of Kokand (1709-1876) rose in the fertile Fergana Valley, fought off Dzungar invasions, and grew rich on irrigated agriculture and the trade between India and Russia - until Russian armies abolished it in 1876.
pageData.para4: The khanates' world ended with the Russian conquest of Central Asia: Kokand annexed in 1876, Khiva and Bukhara reduced to protectorates, and both finally extinguished in 1920. But the Uzbek name they carried - from Abu'l-Khayr's steppe horde - lives on in modern Uzbekistan.

pageData.title: The Dzungar Khanate
pageData.para1: The Dzungar Khanate. The Dzungar Khanate (1634-1758) was the last great nomadic empire of the steppe - the state of the Oirat, the western Mongols, who from their homeland in Dzungaria (northern Xinjiang) built a realm stretching from southern Siberia to Tibet. Tibetan Buddhism was its faith, the horse its power, and for a century it stood as the Qing dynasty's most dangerous rival for the mastery of Inner Asia.
pageData.para2: The Oirats united in the Junggar Basin around 1620, and the khanate took shape under Erdeni Batur. Its greatest khans were conquerors: Galdan, who received the title Boshugtu Khan from the Dalai Lama in 1678, conquered the Tarim Basin and crushed the Khalkha Mongols before the Qing defeated him and stripped him of Outer Mongolia in 1696. His successor Tsewang Rabtan went further - in 1717 Dzungar cavalry seized Lhasa itself, holding Tibet until the Qing drove them out in 1720. Under Galdan Tseren (r. 1727-1745) the khanate's armies ranged as far west as Tashkent and the Fergana Valley.
pageData.para3: The end came from within. After Galdan Tseren's death the khanate tore itself apart in civil war - and the Qing emperor Qianlong saw his chance. Between 1755 and 1758 Qing armies conquered Dzungaria and, in a campaign of annihilation remembered as the Dzungar genocide, wiped out the Dzungar people - a whole nation erased from its homeland.
pageData.para4: The destruction of the Dzungars redrew the map of Asia: it opened the way to the Qing conquest of Mongolia and Tibet, and created 'Xinjiang' - the 'New Frontier' - as a province of China on the emptied land. The last nomadic empire of the steppe had fallen, and with it ended the age when horsemen could challenge empires.

pageData.title: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia
pageData.para1: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia. The Russian conquest of Central Asia (1717-1895) turned the map of a continent: in a century and a half, the Tsar's armies absorbed the steppe of the Kazakh khans, the oasis khanates of Bukhara, Khiva, and Kokand, and the Turkmen desert - creating Russian Turkestan and bringing the Russian Empire to the borders of Afghanistan, Persia, and China. It was the Central Asian half of the Great Game.
pageData.para2: The steppe came first. Through the 18th and 19th centuries Russia pushed its line of forts deeper into the Kazakh grasslands; the abolition of the Kazakh khanate in the 1820s provoked Kenesary Qasymuly's ten-year rebellion, crushed by 1847. Fort by fort - the Turgay, the Irgiz, Fort Raim on the Syr Darya - the Russians advanced, completing the Syr-Darya Line by 1864.
pageData.para3: The main event followed at once: in 1864-1868 the Russians drove south into the settled zone. Tashkent fell in June 1865 after Chernayev's night storm of its walls; Samarkand followed in 1868. The Khanate of Kokand was penned into the Fergana Valley and annexed outright in 1876; the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Khiva survived only as Russian protectorates. The pattern was the same everywhere: Russian breech-loading rifles and artillery shattering armies many times their size.
pageData.para4: The conquest ended in the 1880s-90s with the absorption of the Turkmen lands and the fixing of the Afghan frontier: Russia and Britain, rivals in the Great Game, agreed to leave Afghanistan as a neutral buffer between their empires. Russian Turkestan passed to the Soviets after 1917 and remained Moscow's domain until 1991, when its five republics - Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan - became independent states.

pageData.title: The Mughal Empire
pageData.para1: The Mughal Empire. The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) was the last great imperial power of pre-colonial India - at its height ruling most of the Indian subcontinent. It was founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley, who defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at the First Battle of Panipat. His son Humayun lost the new empire to the Afghan Sher Shah Suri and fled to Persia, but returned in triumph in 1555; after his accidental death the next year, his young son Akbar inherited the throne.
pageData.para2: Akbar (r. 1556-1605) made the conquest an empire: he extended Mughal rule over almost the whole subcontinent north of the Godavari, built a centralized administration and a silver currency, taxed the land through a regulated revenue system, and won over the Hindu Rajput elites with office and alliance. His court experimented with religious dialogue - even a new imperial cult, the Din-i Ilahi. Under his grandson Shah Jahan, the empire reached its architectural apogee: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort, and Fatehpur Sikri remain among the wonders of the world, and Mughal peace made 17th-century India an expanding economic giant feeding Europe's hunger for its textiles and goods.
pageData.para3: The empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) - and broke under the strain. His endless Deccan wars exhausted the treasury; after his death the empire hollowed out with astonishing speed: Nader Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried off the Peacock Throne, the Marathas and provincial dynasties carved up the provinces, and by 1760 the emperor ruled little beyond Delhi itself, a pensioner in all but name of whoever held the city - increasingly, the British.
pageData.para4: The end came in 1857: when the great rebellion against the East India Company was crushed, the last Mughal, the aged poet-emperor Bahadur Shah II, was deposed and exiled, and the British Crown assumed direct rule of India. The Mughal legacy is India itself - its administration, its cuisine and language, and the monuments, from Humayun's Tomb to the Taj, that the whole world comes to see.

pageData.title: The Maratha Confederacy
pageData.para1: The Maratha Confederacy. The Maratha Confederacy (1674-1818) was the power that broke the Mughal Empire - a Hindu warrior state from the western Deccan that grew, in a single century, from a mountain revolt into the master of a third of the Indian subcontinent. Its founder was Shivaji, the legendary guerrilla king who defied both the Sultanate of Bijapur and the Mughals of Aurangzeb to found 'Hindavi Swarajya' - self-rule - crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. Aurangzeb spent the last quarter-century of his reign trying to crush the Marathas and bled his empire white in the attempt.
pageData.para2: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Maratha flood swept north under the Peshwas - the hereditary prime ministers at Pune who became the state's real rulers. Peshwa Bajirao I expanded the Maratha realm deep into northern India; by 1737 the Marathas, while still nominally acknowledging the Mughal emperor, in practice controlled Mughal politics. The confederacy took its mature form: the Peshwa at Pune leading four great independent Maratha houses - the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore, the Bhonsle of Nagpur, and the Gaekwad of Baroda - ruling some two and a half million square kilometers.
pageData.para3: The high tide broke at Panipat: in 1761 the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan crushed the Maratha army at Panipat. Yet within ten years Peshwa Madhavrao I had recovered most of the lost ground. What the Afghans could not do, the Marathas did to themselves: after the Peshwa's authority collapsed in civil strife, the defeated Peshwa Baji Rao II threw himself on British protection in 1802.
pageData.para4: That was the end. The great houses resisted the Company's encroachment in the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars, and by 1818 the confederacy was destroyed, its lands absorbed into British India. The last power that could have built an Indian empire from within was gone - and the road to the British Raj lay open.

pageData.title: The British East India Company
pageData.para1: The British East India Company. The British East India Company (1600-1874) was the strangest empire in history: a private joint-stock company that conquered a subcontinent. Chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on the last day of 1600 with a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, it began as a spice venture - but Dutch competition in the East Indies drove it to India, where a naval victory over the Portuguese at Swally in 1612 won it Mughal favor and its first mainland footholds.
pageData.para2: For a century and a half it was a trading company pure and simple - and a colossally successful one: by the mid-1700s it accounted for half of world trade in cotton, silk, indigo, saltpetre, tea, and later opium. Then it became a state. At Plassey in 1757 its army defeated the Nawab of Bengal, and province by province - by treaty, intrigue, and war - the Company swallowed the subcontinent. At its peak it was the largest corporation in the world, with three presidency armies totaling some 260,000 soldiers, at times twice the size of the British Army itself.
pageData.para3: Company rule was extraction: its taxes, wrung from the countryside by force, impoverished Bengal - where company policy helped turn drought into the Great Famine of 1770, in which an estimated ten million people starved - while its opium trade with China added another notorious stream of profit.
pageData.para4: The reckoning came in 1857: the great rebellion of the Company's own Indian soldiers shook its rule to its foundations. When the smoke cleared, Parliament ended the experiment: the Government of India Act 1858 transferred everything - armies, provinces, revenues - to the British Crown, and the British Raj began. The Company itself lingered as a trading shell until 1874, when it was dissolved. But its century of rule had already decided India's fate for the next two hundred years.

pageData.title: The British Raj
pageData.para1: The British Raj. The British Raj (1858-1947) was the ninety years when the British Crown ruled India directly - the final, most complete, and most consequential chapter of European empire in Asia. It began after the great rebellion of 1857: by the Government of India Act of 1858, the East India Company's vast conquests passed to Queen Victoria, who in 1876 was proclaimed Empress of India. A viceroy governed from Calcutta - after 1911 from the new imperial capital of New Delhi - ruling both the directly administered provinces of British India and, through 'paramountcy,' the hundreds of princely states whose maharajas kept their thrones under British suzerainty.
pageData.para2: The Raj was an empire of superlatives and contradictions. It unified the subcontinent under one administration, one army, and one railway network; it also drained India's wealth to Britain - as Indian nationalists charged - through unfair trade, restraint of Indian industry, and taxes paying British salaries. At its greatest extent it embraced nearly all of today's India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar, with Aden and the Persian Gulf states attached at various times.
pageData.para3: Indian nationalism grew up inside the Raj's own institutions: the Indian National Congress, founded in Bombay in 1885 by Western-educated professionals, moved from loyal petition to the demand for self-rule; the Muslim League followed in 1906; and after the First World War the freedom struggle became a mass movement that no viceroy could contain.
pageData.para4: The end came at midnight on 14-15 August 1947: the Raj was partitioned into two dominions, India and Pakistan, and independence came with the catastrophe of Partition - millions uprooted, and hundreds of thousands dead in communal violence. Burma had already been separated in 1937. The Raj's legacy still defines South Asia: its borders, its English language and institutions - and the unresolved wounds of 1947.

pageData.title: The Ayutthaya Kingdom
pageData.para1: The Ayutthaya Kingdom. The Ayutthaya Kingdom (1351-1767) was the great kingdom of Siam, the forerunner of modern Thailand - and one of the richest and most cosmopolitan states in early modern Asia. Founded on an island in the Chao Phraya river in 1351, it began as a maritime confederation of city-states drawing tribute from the post-Srivijaya world, then centralized over two centuries into a powerful kingdom. European travellers in the early 1500s ranked Ayutthaya one of the three great powers of Asia, alongside Vijayanagara and Ming China.
pageData.para2: Ayutthaya fought its neighbors for centuries - above all Burma. It was a vassal of the Burmese Toungoo empire from 1569 to 1584 before regaining its independence, and in the following centuries its culture flourished. In the seventeenth century the city became a great centre of international trade: under King Narai (r. 1657-1688), Persian and then European influence was strong, and a Siamese embassy dazzled the court of Louis XIV in 1686. The kingdom's later years, built on booming Chinese trade, have been called a golden age of Siamese culture.
pageData.para3: The same period brought danger. Ayutthaya never settled a reliable order of succession, and its elite quarrels weakened the kingdom just as Burma's new Konbaung dynasty rose. Burmese armies invaded in 1759-1760 and again in 1765, and after a fourteen-month siege, on 7 April 1767, Ayutthaya fell. The city was destroyed so completely that the 417-year-old kingdom ended with it - its libraries, palaces, and temples burned.
pageData.para4: Siam recovered with remarkable speed: within fifteen years the Siamese had reunited under new capitals at Thonburi and then Bangkok. But Ayutthaya was never rebuilt, and its monumental ruins stand today as the kingdom's memorial - the remains of what was once one of the largest and most splendid cities in the world.

pageData.title: The Konbaung Kingdom
pageData.para1: The Konbaung Kingdom. The Konbaung dynasty (1752-1885) was the last royal house of Burma - the 'Third Burmese Empire' - and its story is the story of a proud kingdom ground down by the British Empire. It was founded in 1752 by Alaungpaya, a village headman from Shwebo who rose against the Mon conquerors of the fallen Toungoo dynasty, reunified Burma by 1757, and built the second-largest empire in Burmese history, ruling at its height some three million subjects under a royal anthem that proclaimed 'The Whole Southern Island Belongs To Him.'
pageData.para2: Under Alaungpaya's heirs - above all the long-reigning Bodawpaya (1782-1819) - Konbaung Burma expanded in every direction, conquering Arakan, invading Siam (and destroying Ayutthaya in 1767), and pressing into Manipur and Assam. The dynasty continued the administrative reforms of its predecessors and laid the foundations of the modern Burmese state, shifting its capital between Ava, Amarapura, and finally the new royal city of Mandalay, founded in 1857.
pageData.para3: Expansion brought collision with British India. Three Anglo-Burmese Wars decided Burma's fate: the first (1824-1826) cost the kingdom Assam, Arakan, and Tenasserim by the Treaty of Yandabo; the second (1852) took Lower Burma; and the third (1885) took everything. In November 1885 British forces occupied Mandalay, deposed King Thibaw - the last Burmese king - and annexed the whole country into the British Raj.
pageData.para4: The annexation of 1885 ended a millennium of Burmese monarchy, and the last dynasty's fall is remembered in Myanmar as a national wound. Burma remained a province of British India until 1937 and did not regain independence until 1948. The Konbaung legacy - Mandalay's palace, the administrative state, and the memory of resistance - still stands at the heart of Burmese national identity.

pageData.title: The Spanish East Indies
pageData.para1: The Spanish East Indies. The Spanish East Indies - Spain's Asian empire, centered on the Philippines - lasted 333 years, from 1565 to 1898, the longest European colonial rule in Southeast Asia. Ferdinand Magellan had reached the islands in 1521 and died at Mactan; the conquest itself began in 1565, when Miguel Lopez de Legazpi sailed from Mexico, took Cebu, and in 1571 founded Manila as the capital. The whole archipelago was named for King Philip II of Spain.
pageData.para2: The Philippines were ruled from across the Pacific: for over 250 years the islands belonged to the Viceroyalty of New Spain, governed from Mexico City, and were tied to America by the Manila galleon - the great annual ships that crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco for two and a half centuries, carrying Mexican silver east and Chinese silk, porcelain, and spices west, in one of history's first truly global trade routes.
pageData.para3: Spanish rule was thin - a small Spanish population ruling through friars and local chiefs - but its cultural impact was enormous: it converted most of the islands to Catholicism, built towns and universities, and welded hundreds of scattered chiefdoms into a single colony. The colony was even a financial drain on Spain, kept alive by an annual silver subsidy from Mexico.
pageData.para4: The end came in 1896-1898: a Philippine revolution rose against Spain, and then the United States defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War. By the Treaty of Paris of December 1898, Spain sold the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars. Three centuries of Spanish rule ended - and the Filipinos, who had already proclaimed their independence, found themselves fighting a new colonizer instead.

pageData.title: The Dutch East Indies
pageData.para1: The Dutch East Indies. The Dutch East Indies - the Netherlands' vast colony in the Indonesian archipelago - was the prize possession of the Dutch Empire and the ancestor of modern Indonesia. It began as the empire of a company: the Dutch East India Company (VOC) had seized the spice trade from the Portuguese in the 1600s and built its capital at Batavia (modern Jakarta). When the bankrupt VOC was dissolved, the Dutch state took its possessions over on the last day of 1799, and the colony proper was born in 1800. A French and British interregnum interrupted Dutch rule during the Napoleonic Wars, but the Netherlands regained the islands in 1816.
pageData.para2: The nineteenth century made it one of the most profitable colonies in the world. Dutch armies fought a long series of wars that brought the whole archipelago - Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, and finally western New Guinea - under one rule. The infamous Cultivation System forced Javanese peasants to grow export crops for the government; later, private plantations poured out coffee, sugar, tea, rubber, and oil for the world market, while Indonesian nationalism began to stir in response.
pageData.para3: The end came fast. Japan overran the islands in 1942, ending Dutch rule in weeks; when Japan surrendered, Indonesian nationalists under Sukarno proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945. Four years of revolution and war followed before the Netherlands conceded, transferring sovereignty at the end of 1949.
pageData.para4: The colony had lasted a century and a half - and Dutch presence in the East Indies had lasted nearly 350 years. Its legacy is modern Indonesia itself: the borders of a nation of seventeen thousand islands were drawn by the map of the Dutch East Indies.

pageData.title: French Indochina & British Malaya
pageData.para1: French Indochina and British Malaya. Mainland Southeast Asia between Siam and the South China Sea was divided in the nineteenth century between two empires. France built French Indochina: beginning with the conquest of southern Vietnam (Cochinchina, 1862) and a protectorate over Cambodia (1863), it consolidated Vietnam, Cambodia, and later Laos (1899) into a single Indochinese Union in 1887, ruled from Saigon and then, after 1902, from Hanoi. France drained the colony's resources - rice, rubber, and opium - while its schools and hospitals served mostly the French and a small native elite.
pageData.para2: Britain built British Malaya: from its base at Penang (1786), it assembled the Straits Settlements - Penang, Malacca, and Singapore - as direct Crown colonies after a period of East India Company control, and extended protectorates over the Malay sultanates. British Malaya became one of the empire's most profitable possessions, the world's largest producer of tin and later rubber, with George Town and Singapore as great entrepot ports.
pageData.para3: Both empires fell to Japan in 1941-1942, and neither fully recovered. In Indochina, Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh proclaimed Vietnamese independence in 1945; France fought to restore its rule and lost everything at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, when the Geneva Conference ended French Indochina and divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.
pageData.para4: In Malaya the end was peaceful: the post-war Malayan Union proved unpopular, the Federation of Malaya replaced it in 1948, and finally on 31 August 1957 Malaya won independence under Tunku Abdul Rahman - joining with Singapore, Sabah, and Sarawak in 1963 to form Malaysia (Singapore left in 1965). The colonial partition of Southeast Asia had given way to the region's modern states.

pageData.title: The Ming Dynasty
pageData.para1: The Ming Dynasty. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was the last native Han dynasty to rule China - and for two and a half centuries one of the largest, richest, and most ordered states on earth. It rose from the wreckage of Mongol rule: Zhu Yuanzhang, a penniless peasant and former Buddhist monk, fought his way from the Red Turban rebellions to the throne, driving the Yuan back to the steppe and founding the Ming at Nanjing in 1368.
pageData.para2: As the Hongwu Emperor, Zhu tried to freeze China into a stable rural order: self-sufficient villages, a million-man standing army, the world's largest dockyards, and a rigid hierarchy of princes and scholar-officials. His son, the Yongle Emperor, seized the throne in 1402 and made Beijing the capital, building the Forbidden City, restoring the Grand Canal - and launching the extraordinary treasure voyages of Admiral Zheng He, whose giant fleets sailed the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa seven times between 1405 and 1433.
pageData.para3: Then China turned inward. After the emperor himself was captured by the Mongols at Tumu in 1449, the voyages stopped, the navy rotted, and forced labor rebuilt the Great Wall into the stone form we know today. Yet the economy boomed: with perhaps 160 to 200 million people, Ming China fed itself on new American crops - maize, potatoes, chilies - and ran on a flood of American silver that poured in through European trade at Macau, making Chinese porcelain and silk the world's most desired goods.
pageData.para4: The silver also killed it. When the global silver supply faltered in the 1630s, taxes became unpayable just as the Little Ice Age brought famine and epidemic. Rebel armies under Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644; the last Ming emperor hanged himself, and the Manchu Qing swept in from the northeast to take the throne. Ming loyalists held out in the south until 1662, but the dynasty's age - the China of the Great Wall, the Forbidden City, and the blue-and-white vase - was over.

pageData.title: The Qing Dynasty
pageData.para1: The Qing Dynasty. The Qing dynasty (1644-1912) was China's last imperial dynasty - and its largest. Founded by the Manchus, a people of the northeast whose leader Nurhaci had unified the Jurchen tribes into the Later Jin state in 1616, the Qing seized Beijing in 1644 when the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to them, then ground down forty years of resistance to complete the conquest of China by 1683.
pageData.para2: Under three extraordinary long-lived emperors the Qing reached its zenith. The Kangxi Emperor (r. 1661-1722) consolidated the empire and patronized Confucian scholarship; the Qianlong Emperor (r. 1735-1796) pushed its frontiers deep into Central Asia, destroying the Dzungar Khanate and adding Xinjiang, Mongolia, and Tibet. At its height the Qing ruled the most territory of any dynasty in Chinese history - in 1790 the fourth-largest empire the world had yet seen - and the most people: over 400 million.
pageData.para3: The nineteenth century brought collapse from without and within. Defeat in the Opium Wars forced China open to unequal treaties, foreign treaty ports, and the 'century of humiliation'; the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) and other revolts killed more than 20 million people; and defeat by Japan in 1895 showed that even Asia no longer feared the dragon throne. Reform came too late and too slowly.
pageData.para4: The end came in 1911-1912: the Xinhai Revolution swept the provinces, and in February 1912 the last emperor - the child Puyi - abdicated, ending not just a dynasty but two thousand years of Chinese monarchy. The Republic of China took over an empire the Qing had assembled, and modern China's borders are still essentially the ones the Manchu emperors drew.

pageData.title: The Opium Wars & Century of Humiliation
pageData.para1: The Opium Wars and the Century of Humiliation. The Opium Wars (1839-1842 and 1856-1860) were the two conflicts that cracked China open to the West - and began the period Chinese remember as the 'century of humiliation.' Their cause was a drug trade. China sold tea, silk, and porcelain to Britain for silver, and British merchants - above all the East India Company, growing opium in Bengal - reversed the flow by smuggling opium into China by the thousands of chests a year, addicting millions and draining the empire's silver.
pageData.para2: When the Daoguang Emperor's commissioner Lin Zexu seized and destroyed 20,000 chests of British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain answered with gunboats. The Royal Navy's steam-powered warships outclassed the Qing forces, and the 1842 Treaty of Nanking - the first of the 'unequal treaties' - forced China to cede Hong Kong, pay 21 million dollars in reparations, and open five treaty ports including Shanghai to foreign trade. France and America soon extracted the same terms.
pageData.para3: The Second Opium War (1856-1860) went further: Britain and France, using a minor incident over the ship Arrow as a pretext, fought their way to Beijing itself, looted and burned the emperor's Old Summer Palace, and imposed the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Peking - opening ten more ports, legalizing the opium trade, allowing Christian missionaries into the interior, and ceding the Kowloon peninsula.
pageData.para4: The wars exposed the Qing empire's weakness to the world - and to itself. For a century afterward, foreign powers dictated terms on Chinese soil, while rebellions and reform movements tore at the dynasty from within. The memory of those decades - taught to every Chinese schoolchild as the century of humiliation - still shapes how China sees the West and itself.

pageData.title: The Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period)
pageData.para1: The Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period). The Tokugawa shogunate (1603-1868) - the Edo period - was 265 years of peace, order, and isolation that made Japan what it is. It began when Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, ending a century of civil war, and took the title of shogun in 1603. For two and a half centuries, the Tokugawa clan ruled Japan from Edo Castle - the future Tokyo - while the emperor remained a powerless figurehead in Kyoto.
pageData.para2: The shoguns built one of history's most tightly ordered societies. The samurai warrior class stood at the top of a fixed four-class hierarchy; the great lords (daimyo) governed their domains but were forced to spend alternate years at Edo, keeping their families as hostages. Christianity was banned, and under the sakoku ('closed country') edicts of the 1630s, Japan shut itself off: no Japanese could leave, and foreigners could enter only through one Dutch trading post at Nagasaki.
pageData.para3: Peace transformed the country. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world; the merchant class rose on rice, silk, and credit; and townspeople created a brilliant urban culture - kabuki theater, ukiyo-e prints, haiku poetry, and the pleasure quarters of the 'floating world.' A samurai-dominated state had produced a merchant's civilization.
pageData.para4: The isolation ended in 1853, when American Commodore Perry's 'black ships' steamed into Edo Bay and demanded Japan open its ports. The shogunate, unable to resist, signed the Kanagawa Treaty of 1854 - and the crisis shattered its authority. Samurai reformers rallied around the emperor, and in 1868 the last shogun fell in the Meiji Restoration. Japan emerged from two centuries of seclusion determined to catch up with the world - and did so in a single generation.

pageData.title: The Meiji Restoration
pageData.para1: The Meiji Restoration. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 was the moment Japan reinvented itself - the fastest and most complete national transformation of the modern age. Fifteen years after Commodore Perry's black ships had forced Japan open, the samurai of the Satsuma and Choshu domains overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and 'restored' the fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji to power on 3 January 1868, promising in the Charter Oath to seek knowledge throughout the world.
pageData.para2: The young leaders around the emperor - mostly lower-ranking samurai in their thirties - dismantled the old world in a single generation. They abolished the feudal domains (1871), ended the samurai class and its privileges, created a national conscript army (1873), and sent the Iwakura Mission around the world to study the West. Railways, telegraphs, banks, factories, and a modern education system followed with astonishing speed.
pageData.para3: The transformation met resistance - most famously the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, when the last great samurai uprising was crushed by the new conscript army it had helped create. (An earlier stand by Tokugawa loyalists, including a short-lived 'Republic of Ezo' in Hokkaido, had already failed in the Boshin War.) By 1889 Japan had the Meiji Constitution and an elected parliament - a framework that lasted until 1947 - and by 1905 - when it defeated Russia - it had become the first non-Western modern great power, with an empire of its own in Korea and Taiwan.
pageData.para4: The Meiji Restoration saved Japan from the fate of China - but it also turned Japan into an empire. The same drive that built the railways and warships carried Japan into wars with China (1894-95) and Russia (1904-05), the annexation of Korea (1910), and ultimately the Pacific War. Modern Japan - its strengths and its tragedies - was born in 1868.

pageData.title: The Joseon Dynasty (Korea)
pageData.para1: The Joseon Dynasty (Korea). The Joseon dynasty (1392-1897) ruled Korea for 505 years - longer than any other royal house of its era - and made Korea in its own image. It was founded by the general Yi Seong-gye, who overthrew the Goryeo kingdom in 1392, took the throne as King Taejo, and moved the capital to Hanseong, modern Seoul. Under his heirs the kingdom pushed its borders north to the Amnok (Yalu) and Tuman rivers - essentially Korea's borders today.
pageData.para2: Joseon remade Korea on Neo-Confucian principles: Buddhism was pushed aside and its followers at times persecuted, and a scholar-official elite (the yangban) governed through civil service examinations. The dynasty's greatest king, Sejong the Great (r. 1418-1450), presided over a golden age of science and culture - and gave Korea its greatest treasure: hangul, the Korean alphabet, promulgated in 1446 so that ordinary people could read and write.
pageData.para3: The kingdom survived its trials. Japan's warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded in 1592 and 1597, devastating the peninsula, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy - with its armored 'turtle ships' - cut Japanese supply lines and saved the kingdom. Manchu invasions in 1627 and 1636-37 forced Joseon to accept Qing overlordship, after which Korea turned inward for nearly two centuries of peace as the 'hermit kingdom.'
pageData.para4: The end came in the age of empire: pressed by Japan, Russia, and the Western powers, King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897, but Japan annexed Korea outright in 1910, ending five centuries of the dynasty. Joseon's legacy - hangul, Confucian institutions, and the Korean nation itself - endured through thirty-five years of Japanese rule and into the two Koreas of today.
